# Part IV: Reasoning and Test-Time Compute {#part-reasoning .unnumbered}

> "... generating a chain of thought ... significantly improves the ability of large
> language models to perform complex reasoning."
>
> Jason Wei et al., ["Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)

In this part, reasoning in a modern model is a way of spending computation
before the answer is fixed, not a separate module inside the network. That extra
computation, spent while the model answers rather than during training, is what
the title calls test-time compute. Sometimes a prompt induces that spending. It
can be organized as search, or delegated to a program, solver, or proof checker.
In other systems the model is trained to reason; in still others the work stays
at inference, where the system samples, checks, branches, or routes by
difficulty before committing to an answer.

@sec-eliciting-reasoning begins with the smallest change: giving the model room
to reason before it answers and not treating a single sample as a reliable
answer. @sec-structured-reasoning-search then makes the control problem explicit: a chain is one path, a tree keeps
alternatives alive, and a graph reuses partial work. @sec-programs-solvers-symbolic
splits reasoning into translation and execution, where the model writes a
program, query, symbolic chain, or proof script and an external runtime computes
or checks it. @sec-verifiers-process-supervision studies the verifier itself,
from unit tests and answer checkers to process reward models and generative
verifiers.

@sec-training-to-reason moves the cost into training, where verifiable rewards
(reward signals taken from answers that can be checked automatically) and
reinforcement learning are used to make useful reasoning habitual rather than ad
hoc. In @sec-reasoning-data-distillation the reasoning traces themselves become
training data: self-generated rationales, rejection sampling, small curated
sets, distillation, and long-to-short transfer. @sec-inference-time-scaling then
treats computation at test time as a budgeted resource: parallel attempts,
sequential refinement, verification, routing by difficulty, and the production
problem of overthinking.

Any reasoning claim can be tested with four questions: where is the extra work
paid for, who checks it, what data records it, and does more computation improve
coverage, selection, or both. Coverage is the chance that at least one attempt
is correct; selection is whether the system then picks a correct attempt. With
those questions answered separately, a prompting method, a reasoning-trained
model, and a test-time scaling system can be compared as engineering options on
the same terms.
